english: to occur, to happen, to arise
usage: The thing that occurs always takes 이/가, never 을/를 — 발생하다 cannot take an object.
발생한 + noun is the modifier form you see in reports: 사고가 발생한 장소/원인 (the place/cause the accident occurred).
Standard medicine/manual warning — 부작용이/이상이 발생하다 (a side effect/abnormality arises).
If a fire breaks out, call 119.
화재가 발생하다 = a fire breaks out; the conditional 발생하면 is the go-to phrasing in safety notices.
examples: 여기서 자주 문제가 발생해요.
Problems often occur here.
Polite 발생해요 — note 하다 contracts 하 + 어 → 해, never 발생하요.
결제 중에 오류가 발생했습니다.
An error occurred during payment.
Formal 발생했습니다 is the exact wording you see on payment screens and system error pages.
작은 실수가 큰 사고로 발생할 수도 있어요.
A small mistake can turn into a big accident.
Real-situation caution — pairs 발생할 수도 있다 (might possibly occur) with the ~(으)로 'into' marker.
nuance: 발생하다 (發生, 'issue-forth + arise') is the formal, written-leaning verb for an event, problem, or phenomenon coming into existence — accidents, errors, fires, costs, side effects, diseases. The everyday near-synonym is 생기다, and the dividing line is register and scale: 문제가 생겼어요 is what you say to a friend, while 문제가 발생했어요 belongs to news, reports, manuals, and official notices. Crucially it is intransitive — the thing that occurs takes 이/가, so you can never 'occur something' (no 발생하다 with 을/를). The classic English-speaker trap is translating 'cause a problem' as 문제를 발생하다; Korean instead says 문제가 발생하다 (a problem arises) or, for an agent making it happen, 문제를 일으키다. Remember 하다 contracts to 해요 — 발생하요 is a spelling error.

mistakes: Don't use it transitively — say 문제가 발생했어요 (a problem occurred), not 문제를 발생했어요; for 'cause a problem' use 문제를 일으키다.
Writing 발생하요 instead of 발생해요 — every 하다 verb contracts 하 + 어 to 해, so the polite form is 발생해요.
Using it for tiny personal events sounds robotic — say 배가 고파졌어요, not 배고픔이 발생했어요; reserve 발생하다 for incidents, errors, and reports.

usage: 존재하지 않아요 is the natural way to deny existence flatly — 'there's no such thing.'
The thing that exists takes 이/가 — 존재하다 is intransitive and cannot take an object.
존재할까요? frames a big, abstract yes/no question — philosophy, religion, science.
그 회사는 더 이상 존재하지 않아요.
더 이상 + 존재하지 않다 = no longer exists — for things that have ceased to be.
examples: 산타클로스는 정말 존재해?
Does Santa Claus really exist?
Casual 존재해? to a child or friend — the contracted 하 + 어 → 해 form.
그 문제는 오래전부터 존재했어요.
That problem has existed for a long time.
오래전부터 존재했어요 stresses a problem has 'been there' all along, not just appeared.
편견은 여전히 우리 사회에 존재합니다.
Prejudice still exists in our society.
Formal 존재합니다 with 여전히 (still) fits essays and serious discussion about society.
nuance: 존재하다 (存在, 'remain + be present') means 'to exist' in an abstract, weighty, or emphatic sense — common in writing, debate, philosophy, and serious topics. Its everyday near-synonym is 있다, and the line is sharp: for 'there is / I have' you must use 있다 (책이 있어요, 질문이 있어요), never 존재하다. Reach for 존재하다 only when you want to spotlight the very fact of something's existence — a method, a being, a problem — or to deny it categorically with 존재하지 않아요. It is intransitive, so the thing that exists takes 이/가 and there is no object. The big English-speaker pitfall is mapping every English 'exist/there is' onto 존재하다: 'there's a café nearby' is 근처에 카페가 있어요, and saying 카페가 존재해요 sounds comically grand. Keep 존재하다 for the abstract and the philosophical.

The natural negative is 존재하지 않아요; clipping it to 존재 안 해요 sounds off-register for such an abstract verb.
Treating it as transitive — there is no 존재하다 with 을/를; the existing thing always takes 이/가 (생명체가 존재하다).

english: to develop, to advance, to progress
usage: The thing that develops takes 이/가 — 발전하다 is intransitive (기술이/경제가 발전하다).
~(으)로 발전하다 = 'develop INTO': 연인으로, 큰 문제로, 사업으로 — the target takes (으)로.
I want to develop the country.
To develop something on purpose, switch to the transitive 발전시키다 (을/를): 경제를 발전시키다.
The company has grown a lot.
회사가/도시가 발전하다 = an organization or place grows and advances — positive, intransitive.
examples: 우리 동네가 많이 발전했어.
Our neighborhood has developed a lot.
Casual 발전했어 — for places and economies visibly growing over time.
꾸준히 하면 실력이 발전할 거예요.
If you keep at it, your skills will improve.
실력이 발전하다 = one's skills advance — an encouraging line about steady progress.
작은 다툼이 큰 싸움으로 발전했어요.
A small spat escalated into a big fight.
Real-situation — 발전하다 can mean a situation escalates ~(으)로 into something bigger, often negative.
nuance: 발전하다 (發展, 'issue-forth + unfold/spread') means to move to a more advanced, mature, or larger stage — technology, economies, skills, companies, even relationships. It is normally intransitive (실력이 발전하다, 경제가 발전하다), and the 'into' target takes ~(으)로 (연인으로 발전하다 = develop into lovers). Its near-synonym 성장하다 ('grow') overlaps but leans biological/scale growth (아이가 성장하다 = a child grows up), whereas 발전하다 stresses qualitative advancement to a higher level. The number-one trap for learners is the look-alike 발견하다 (to discover) — one syllable apart and totally unrelated, so 신약을 발전하다 wrongly means 'develop a new drug' when you meant 발견하다 (discover). The second trap is using 발전하다 transitively; to actively develop something you need the causative 발전시키다 (기술을 발전시켰어요), never 기술을 발전했어요.

english: to be improved, to be enhanced
usage: My listening skills have improved a lot.
The thing that improves takes 이/가 — 향상되다 is intransitive (실력이/품질이 향상되다).
I want to improve my skills.
To improve something deliberately, use the transitive 향상시키다 (을/를): 실력을 향상시키다.
Pairs with measurable nouns — 성능이/효율이/품질이 향상되다, often with 크게 (greatly).
삶의 질이 향상되다 = quality of life rises — a set phrase in health and welfare talk.
examples: 매일 연습하니까 발음이 향상됐어.
Since I practice daily, my pronunciation got better.
Casual 향상됐어 — classic study context: 발음이/문법이 향상되다.
업데이트 후 속도가 크게 향상됐습니다.
After the update, the speed greatly improved.
Formal 향상됐습니다 fits product release notes and reviews.
꾸준히 운동하면 체력이 향상될 거예요.
If you exercise regularly, your stamina will improve.
Real-situation advice — 체력이 향상되다 is natural in health and fitness guidance.
nuance: 향상되다 (向上, 'turn-toward + up' + 되다) literally pictures something 'turning upward,' i.e. a skill, quality, or level rising and getting better. It is the intransitive, formal cousin of the everyday 좋아지다 (to get better): 실력이 좋아졌어요 is casual, while 실력이 향상됐어요 sounds polished and is what teachers, reviews, and reports use. Use it for measurable, ratable things — 실력, 품질, 성능, 효율, 체력, 삶의 질 — rather than moods or weather. The key English-speaker pitfall is the active/passive split: 향상되다 means something improved on its own, but if YOU improved it you must use the causative 향상시키다 (실력을 향상시켰어요), never 실력을 향상됐어요. Watch the spelling too: 되어요 contracts to 돼요 and the past is 향상됐어요 — 향상되요 and 향상됬어요 are both wrong.

english: to decrease, to decline, to drop
usage: The population is decreasing every year.
The thing that drops takes 이/가 — 감소하다 is intransitive (인구가/매출이 감소하다).
Pairs with figures — 매출이/수요가 ~% 감소하다 (decreased by ~%); the percentage marks the amount.
To reduce something on purpose, use the transitive 줄이다 (을/를) — 감소하다 itself cannot take an object.
Also works for abstract amounts — 스트레스가/위험이 감소하다 (stress/risk goes down).
examples: 손님이 줄었어.
Fewer customers came.
In casual speech Koreans say 줄다/줄어들다, not 감소하다 — keep 감소하다 for numbers and reports.
출생률이 빠르게 감소하고 있습니다.
The birth rate is declining rapidly.
Formal 감소하고 있습니다 fits news and reports about social trends.
꾸준히 운동하면 질병 위험이 감소할 수 있어요.
Regular exercise can lower the risk of disease.
Real-situation — 위험이 감소하다 (risk decreases) is common in health writing.
nuance: 감소하다 (減少, 'reduce + few') is the formal, statistical verb for an amount or number going down, and it lives in a fixed pair with its opposite 증가하다 (增加, to increase) — the two appear together constantly in news, reports, and graphs. Its everyday near-synonyms are 줄다 and 줄어들다: a Korean tells a friend 손님이 줄었어요, but a report says 고객 수가 감소했습니다. The dividing line is purely register and context (numbers/data → 감소하다; daily talk → 줄다). It is intransitive (이/가), so the big pitfall for English speakers is trying to say 'reduce the cost' as 비용을 감소하다 — that is ungrammatical; to actively cut something you use the transitive 줄이다 (비용을 줄이다) or the causative 감소시키다. Reserve 감소하다 for things that go down on their own in a measured, formal frame.

Don't confuse the 한자 pair — 감소하다 is decrease and 증가하다 is increase; mixing them in a report reverses your meaning entirely.

english: to increase, to rise, to grow
usage: The thing that rises takes 이/가 — 증가하다 is intransitive (관광객이/수출이 증가하다).
Pairs with figures — 수출이/수요가 ~% 증가하다, often with 크게 (significantly).
To increase something on purpose, use the transitive 늘리다 (을/를) — 증가하다 cannot take an object.
증가하는 추세 = 'an increasing trend' — a very common set phrase in reports and articles.
examples: 요즘 손님이 늘었어.
We've had more customers lately.
In casual speech Koreans say 늘다/늘어나다, not 증가하다 — reserve 증가하다 for numbers and reports.
1인 가구가 빠르게 증가하고 있습니다.
Single-person households are rapidly increasing.
Formal 증가하고 있습니다 fits reports on demographic and social trends.
기온이 오르면 전기 사용량이 증가해요.
When the temperature rises, electricity usage goes up.
Real-situation cause-and-effect with measured amounts — 사용량이/소비가 증가하다.
nuance: 증가하다 (增加, 'add + add') is the formal, statistical verb for an amount or number rising, and it pairs directly with its mirror 감소하다 (減少, to decrease) throughout news, data, and graphs. Its everyday near-synonyms are 늘다 and 늘어나다: a friend hears 손님이 늘었어요, while a report states 매출이 증가했습니다 — same event, different register. It is intransitive (이/가). The chief English-speaker pitfall is the active/passive confusion baked into English 'increase,' which is both transitive and intransitive: in Korean you cannot 'increase the staff' as 직원을 증가하다 — for the deliberate act you switch to the transitive 늘리다 (인원을 늘리다) or the causative 증가시키다. So a thing rises on its own with 증가하다, but a person enlarges it with 늘리다. Keep 증가하다 for measured, report-style contexts.

english: to maintain, to keep, to sustain
usage: I exercise daily to maintain my health.
유지하다 is transitive — the thing you keep takes 을/를 (건강을/온도를 유지하다).
Please keep it at the right temperature.
Common with conditions and levels — 온도를/거리를/관계를 유지하다.
The condition is being kept well.
For 'stay as is / be maintained' on its own, use the passive 유지되다 (이/가): 상태가 유지되다.
거리를 유지하다 = keep a (physical or social) distance — a fixed safety/etiquette phrase.
examples: 체온을 유지해.
Keep your body warm.
Casual 유지해 — to a friend; 체온을 유지하다 = maintain body temperature.
좋은 성적을 유지하기가 쉽지 않아요.
It's not easy to keep up good grades.
성적을 유지하다 = keep up grades; ~기가 쉽지 않다 = 'it's not easy to.'
두 나라는 우호 관계를 유지하고 있습니다.
The two countries maintain friendly relations.
Real-situation/news — 관계를 유지하다 = sustain a relationship, formal register.
nuance: 유지하다 (維持, 'tie/hold + grasp') means to keep something the way it is so it doesn't change, slip, or decline — health, temperature, grades, balance, distance, relationships. Unlike its look-alike-in-meaning 지키다 (to protect/keep a promise: 약속을 지키다), 유지하다 is about sustaining a state or level over time rather than guarding or defending. It is transitive, so the thing maintained takes 을/를 (거리를 유지하다 = keep your distance), and the big English-speaker trap is mapping 'is maintained' onto the same word — for the intransitive 'stays as is / is kept' you must switch to 유지되다 (상태가 유지되다). A second pitfall is the look-alike 유치하다, which is unrelated (it means 'childish' or 'to attract/host,' as in 올림픽을 유치하다). 유지하다 carries a mildly formal tone but is everyday in health and habit advice.

Don't use it for keeping a promise — that's 약속을 지키다 (지키다), while 유지하다 is for sustaining a state or level.

english: to form, to shape, to build up
usage: For things forming on their own, the passive 형성되다 (이/가) is most natural: 성격이 형성되다.
형성하다 is transitive — what you build up takes 을/를 (습관을/관계를 형성하다).
집단을/공동체를 형성하다 = form a group/community — abstract, structural formation.
여론을 형성하다 = shape public opinion — a set phrase in formal writing about society.
examples: 새로운 관계를 형성하는 데 시간이 걸려요.
It takes time to form new relationships.
관계를 형성하다 = build a relationship; ~는 데 시간이 걸리다 = 'it takes time to.'
이 지역은 오래전에 형성됐어요.
This area was formed long ago.
For places or layers forming naturally, the intransitive 형성되다 is standard.
여러 의견이 모여 여론을 형성합니다.
Various opinions come together to form public opinion.
Real-situation/formal — 의견이 모여 여론을 형성하다, common in essays about society.
nuance: 형성하다 (形成, 'shape/form + complete') means to form or build something up over time — a personality, a habit, a relationship, a group, a market, public opinion. It is abstract and written-leaning. Its everyday counterpart 만들다 ('make') is for concrete, physical objects (밥을 만들다 = make rice), whereas 형성하다 is reserved for gradual, structural, often intangible formation; saying 밥을 형성하다 is simply wrong. The transitive 형성하다 takes 을/를, but the crucial nuance for learners is that Korean strongly prefers the passive 형성되다 for things that come about on their own (성격이 형성되다 = personality is formed, not 성격을 형성하다), using the active form only when a clear agent deliberately shapes something (그들이 여론을 형성했다). So choose 형성하다 vs 형성되다 by asking whether someone is actively doing the shaping or it simply happens.

Don't use 형성하다 to make a physical object — '밥을 형성하다' is wrong; use 만들다 for concrete things.
Don't confuse it with 형성하다's look-alike 결성하다 (to band together / form a group like a band) — 밴드를 결성하다 vs the broader 형성하다.

english: to compose, to organize, to make up
usage: I organized the team with five people.
Transitive: the whole takes 을/를, the parts take (으)로 — 팀을 다섯 명으로 구성하다.
이 책은 세 부분으로 구성돼 있어요.
This book is made up of three parts.
Very common as the passive — X(으)로 구성되어 있다 = 'consists of / is made up of X.'
Please arrange the menu as a course.
~(으)로 구성하다 = arrange/organize into a form — natural for menus, programs, plans.
I structured the presentation to be easy to follow.
내용을 구성하다 = structure the content — useful for work and study.
examples: 조를 두 명씩 구성해.
Make groups of two each.
Casual 구성해 — 두 명씩 (in twos); 조를 구성하다 = form teams/groups.
우리 동아리는 다양한 사람들로 구성돼 있어요.
Our club is made up of diverse people.
X(으)로 구성되어 있다 is the standard way to say 'is composed of X.'
회사는 다섯 개 부서로 구성되어 있습니다.
The company consists of five departments.
Real-situation/formal — 부서로 구성되어 있다, common in introductions and reports.
nuance: 구성하다 (構成, 'construct + complete') means to put something together out of parts — a team, a menu, a program, the structure of a presentation. The grammar is the heart of it: the whole takes 을/를 and the components take (으)로 (팀을 다섯 명으로 구성하다 = make up a team out of five people). It overlaps with 조직하다 (組織, to organize/establish, e.g. 위원회를 조직하다), but 구성하다 emphasizes the part-to-whole make-up while 조직하다 emphasizes founding a structured body. By far the most common form you will meet is the passive 구성되다 in the fixed frame X(으)로 구성되어 있다 ('consists of / is made up of X'). The recurring English-speaker pitfall is marking the parts with 을/를 like an English object — '세 명을 구성하다' is wrong; the people are the material, so they take (으)로: 세 명으로 구성하다.

english: to apply, to put into use
usage: Transitive: what you apply takes 을/를 — 할인을/규칙을/이론을 적용하다.
We apply the new rule to all employees.
~에/에게 적용하다 = apply TO a target: 모든 직원에게, 이 경우에.
The passive 적용되다 ('be applied / apply / take effect') is very common for rules and discounts.
The changed fee applies from next month.
다음 달부터 적용되다 = takes effect from next month — standard notice wording.
examples: 배운 거 실제로 적용해 봐.
Try actually applying what you learned.
Casual 적용해 봐 — 내용을/이론을 적용하다, common study advice.
할인이 자동으로 적용됐어요.
The discount was applied automatically.
Everyday shopping — the passive 할인이 적용되다 (a discount is applied) is the natural phrasing.
새 정책은 모든 부서에 동일하게 적용됩니다.
The new policy applies equally to all departments.
Real-situation/formal — 정책이 ~에 적용되다, with the target marked by 에.
nuance: 적용하다 (適用, 'suitable + use') means to apply a rule, discount, theory, or method so it actually takes effect — the thing applied takes 을/를 and the target takes 에/에게 (새 규칙을 직원에게 적용하다). You will meet the passive 적용되다 ('is applied / applies / takes effect') just as often, as in 할인이 적용돼요 or 다음 달부터 적용됩니다. The number-one English-speaker trap is the look-alike 적응하다 (適應, to adjust/adapt to a new environment), which differs by one syllable and is intransitive: 새 회사에 적응했어요 means 'adapted to a new company,' while 새 규칙을 적용했어요 means 'applied a new rule' — mixing them produces nonsense. A second trap is marking the target with 을/를: the rule itself takes 을/를, but the case or person it applies to takes 에/에게 (이 경우에 적용하다, not 이 경우를 적용하다).

english: to carry out, to conduct, to implement
usage: Transitive: the planned activity takes 을/를 — 조사를/교육을/정책을 실시하다. Formal register.
We will conduct safety training next week.
Common with organized events — 교육을/검사를/조사를 실시하다.
Construction is scheduled to be carried out from next month.
The passive 실시되다 ('be carried out') is common in formal announcements.
정책을 실시하다 = put a policy into effect — typical government/official wording.
examples: 숙제를 했어.
I did my homework.
For personal everyday tasks use plain 하다 — never 실시하다; 실시하다 is only for official, organized undertakings.
정부가 새 정책을 실시했습니다.
The government implemented a new policy.
Formal 실시했습니다 — 정책을 실시하다 is standard news and official phrasing.
회사는 매년 건강 검진을 실시합니다.
The company carries out health checkups every year.
Real-situation/organizational — 검진을/점검을 실시하다 (conduct checkups/inspections).
nuance: 실시하다 (實施, 'actual + carry out') means to officially put a planned activity into effect — a survey, training, an exam, a policy, an inspection. It is formal and organizational, the language of governments, companies, and schools, not personal life. Its near-synonym 진행하다 (進行, to proceed with / run) overlaps but is broader and more neutral (회의를 진행하다 = run a meeting), whereas 실시하다 specifically frames the formal launch or enforcement of a scheme. It is transitive (을/를), and the passive 실시되다 ('is carried out / takes effect') is frequent in notices. The classic English-speaker pitfall is over-applying English 'do/carry out' to everyday actions: 'I did my homework' is 숙제를 했어요, and 숙제를 실시했어요 sounds absurdly bureaucratic — reserve 실시하다 for official, scheduled undertakings.

english: to solve, to resolve, to settle
usage: We need to solve the problem quickly.
Transitive — the problem takes 을/를; 문제를 해결하다 is the core collocation.
The passive 해결되다 ('be solved / work out') is very common: 문제가 해결되다.
We settled the conflict through dialogue.
갈등을 해결하다 = settle a conflict; 대화로 = 'through conversation' (방법 marked by (으)로).
제가 해결할게요 = 'I'll handle it' — a confident, reassuring everyday line.
examples: 이거 내가 해결할게.
I'll sort this out.
Casual 해결할게 — the ~(으)ㄹ게 promise form, very natural for offering to handle something.
이 앱으로 대부분의 문제를 해결할 수 있어요.
You can solve most problems with this app.
문제를 해결하다 + ~(으)ㄹ 수 있다 = 'can solve' — the everyday workhorse collocation.
양측이 협상으로 갈등을 해결했습니다.
Both sides resolved the conflict through negotiation.
Real-situation/formal — 갈등을 해결하다 covers disputes broadly, not just puzzles.
nuance: 해결하다 (解決, 'untie + decide/settle') is both the everyday and the formal verb for solving or settling a problem, conflict, or situation — its overwhelming partner is 문제 (문제를 해결하다). It is transitive (을/를), and its passive 해결되다 means a matter gets resolved or works out (문제가 해결됐어요). The key contrast English speakers need is with 풀다, which also translates as 'solve' but is literal-'untie' and applies to puzzles, math, riddles, and even stress or misunderstandings (수학 문제를 풀다, 오해를 풀다); 해결하다 covers real-life problems, disputes, and situations more broadly and abstractly. The usual pitfall is the active/passive mix: 'the problem was solved' is 문제가 해결됐어요 (passive 해결되다), not 문제가 해결했어요 — the active 해결하다 needs a solver and an object (제가 문제를 해결했어요).

english: to take up, to occupy, to account for
usage: Food costs take up half of my living expenses.
Transitive — the share taken takes 을/를; the whole it's part of takes ~의 (생활비의 절반을).
Second sense: 'win/secure' a rank or spot — 1위를/우승을/정상을 차지하다.
The luggage takes up too much space.
자리를 차지하다 = take up space or a seat — the literal, everyday physical sense.
It accounts for a large share.
비중을 차지하다 = account for a proportion — a set phrase in statistics and budgets.
examples: 가방이 자리 다 차지했어.
The bag took up the whole spot.
Casual 차지했어 — the literal 'take up space' sense, here a bag hogging a seat.
주거비가 지출에서 큰 부분을 차지해요.
Housing costs make up a large part of spending.
큰 부분을 차지하다 = account for a large share — common in budget talk.
그 가수가 음원 차트 1위를 차지했습니다.
That singer took the number one spot on the music chart.
Real-situation — 1위를 차지하다 for rankings and charts; here in formal news register.
nuance: 차지하다 (a native Korean verb, not Sino-Korean) carries two everyday senses: to take up a proportion or amount (식비가 절반을 차지하다 = food is half the cost) and to secure or win a position (1위를 차지하다 = take first place). It is transitive — the share or prize taken takes 을/를, and when you name the whole it belongs to, that whole takes ~의 (지출의 큰 부분을 차지하다). The first sense is the natural way to say 'X accounts for Y%' in budgets and statistics; the second is the chart/sports/competition sense. The key contrast English speakers miss is with 이기다 (to beat an opponent): 차지하다 is about securing the rank, share, or seat itself, not about defeating someone, so 1위를 차지하다 ('took first') is different from 상대를 이겼다 ('beat the opponent'). Don't confuse it either with 차치하다, a rare formal verb meaning 'to set aside (a topic).'
